title: There Was One Miraculous (Short) Adventure in the Clown Shoe

body_markdown:
Last week, I wrote about coming to terms with selling my 20-year-owned BMW M Coupe. I’d contacted a friend who had dibs on it from when I flirted with selling it three years ago, offering it to him for $25K, and having him balk when I sent a detailed description of its needs and quirks, which included a balky driver’s-side window regulator, an odd elongation of one of the jack pad holes in the rocker panel, and the fact that the car had been repainted even though the CarFax showed no accidents. I then floated it for sale, first on my own Facebook page, then in two BMW enthusiast groups. This generated interest but no meaningful dialog, so I swallowed hard and listed it on Facebook Marketplace with its attendant waterfall of messages containing only an insulting sight-unseen offer or the insufferable “Is it available?”


Even though the first sentence of my ad read, “ALL SIGHT-UNSEEN OFFERS AND IS-IT-AVAILABLES WILL BE IGNORED,” the first response was “$21k” (no accompanying words, just $21k), the second was “Is it available?” and the third was the laughable “Why is it priced so high $10k maybe for a 27 year old BMW with 109k miles,” for which I’m trademarking the new acronym “IYDKYDK.” Every time you use it, you owe me a quarter.


But then some real responses began coming in, including three from people within striking distance. A guy in Albany asked good questions, and I provided the kind of candid answers and warts-and-all description that I would want if I were about to drive from Albany. (Few things are more frustrating than spending hours driving to look at a car, and knowing within 30 seconds that it was a complete waste of time and could’ve been avoided had the seller simply been honest.) Only when he crossed the Rubicon to scheduling the appointment did he respectfully probe how firm I was on the price.


Then he did the “crime of opportunity” thing and hopped in his daily driver and drove out to have a look, and we worked it out. He’s thrilled to be getting the car for a price at which he never thought he’d be able to buy into an M Coupe, and I’m happy to have sold the car for what I consider to be exactly the right price when all of its quirks are fully and ethically disclosed. He left me with a hefty deposit ensuring that neither of us will flake out. I’m expecting a bank check with the balance to arrive in the mail any day. The car is still here while he figures out the get-it-home logistics. All transactions should go like this.


I’ll enjoy seeing that fat planted butt in my driveway for another week.


Rob Siegel


And, as I said last week, this, like selling the previous three cars, isn’t about being in financial straits or bad health. It’s just me selling cars I haven’t been driving much for the past X number of years and reaping the benefit of simplification. The fact that along with it comes reduced financial pressure is a good thing, too.


But really, more than wrapping up the story of selling the car, I wanted to correct something I said last week—that never having taken a real road trip in the M Coupe deprived me of the kind of deep experience that creates a bond with a car. Of course there was the Magnus Walker episode ([article here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/the-urban-outlaw-the-hack-mechanic-and-four-old-tires/) ,[video here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d1AwCMgGen0) ), but there was also an adventure that, while short, was far deeper.


In 2010, my oldest son Ethan was in college, majoring in English and interested in a film career. While he was home for the summer, he entered the 48 Hour Film Project. This is a crazy thing where you’re assigned a topic, then have 48 hours to write, shoot, edit, and submit a sub-15-minute film. The teams all meet in a location (in this case, a bar in downtown Boston) at 7:30 p.m. on a Friday, are given topics, and have until 7:30 p.m. on Sunday to return with a thumb drive containing the finished film.


His team drew “heist film” as the topic. A dozen kids descended on our house and came up with the idea of a botched drug deal. Two of them ran out to Walmart to buy a safe. Maire Anne and I donated cardboard building blocks that our kids used to play with to the project, and some of the other team members painted them white and wrapped them in Saran Wrap to make them look like drugs. A corner of the basement in my mother’s house was repurposed to make it look like a lab. Someone showed up with a watermelon that they then bludgeoned with a baseball bat. It was all brimming with the wonderful energy of youthful creativity and passion.


Ethan asked me if he could use one of “the cool cars” in the film. We decided on the M Coupe, but to keep the insurance costs down on the car, I had previously excluded him from the policy, and I didn’t want to hand the keys to one of the other kids, so I accompanied them over to my mother’s house in Brighton (the outskirts of Boston) where most of the filming was. Ethan concocted a sequence where he’d film an actor exiting the house and getting into the car, and then he’d cut, the actor would get out, I’d get in, they’d resume filming, and I’d pull away from the curb. However, when we tried this, it didn’t look right. I said that I had no objection if the actor pulled away from the curb as long as he was careful. It was a narrow one-way street, so I felt that the odds of anything going wrong were small.


So Ethan tried filming it again. When the actor came out of my mother’s house, I saw a car coming down the street, but it was a good way off. The actor got into my M Coupe and started it. I restrained myself from playing the nervous, overly-protective owner, as I was certain someone would see the approaching car and yell, “Cut!” But no one did. To my horror, the actor began pulling out in front of the approaching car. I shrieked, “ *STOP!* ” Fortunately, he did. The M Coupe’s right front fender and the car’s bumper had less than a foot of daylight between them.


The kid was shaken and embarrassed. He said, “Do you just want to drive it instead of me?” I said, “I have no objection if you pull out from the curb, *but you need to look for traffic, just like you would any other time in any other car.* ” He nodded sheepishly. The second time, it was free of drama, and my blood pressure returned to normal.


The one pic I can find from the film shoot. That’s Ethan, the M Coupe in the foreground, and yes, he’s clubbing a watermelon with a baseball bat. Like I said, the wonderful energy of youthful creative passion.


Rob Siegel


But that’s not the story. It’s what happened after everything was done.


The team spent the day Saturday filming, and Saturday night and Sunday editing. Some crew members were up all night. The thumb drive with the completed film needed to be handed in at the bar in downtown Boston, which Google Maps estimated at a highly optimistic 12 minutes from my house. Still, there would be no problem as long as we didn’t leave at the last minute.


But when, at 6 p.m., Ethan tried a test export of the film to his 4 GB thumb drive (hey, it was 2010), he found that it wouldn’t fit. I volunteered to go find a bigger drive. Running madly between stores in Brighton and Allston, I found an 8 GB drive and beat it back home by 6:45. It was getting tight, but it certainly seemed doable.


Ethan began the final export and was greeted with the slowest-moving progress bar Windows 7 has ever shown. The clock ticked to 7:00. 7:10. 7:15. The unthinkable—not being able to get the movie submitted on time—was turning into a reality.


Finally, at 7:20, the export was done. Ethan double-clicked on the exported file to make sure it played (not that there was time to do anything if it didn’t), grabbed the thumb drive, and the both of us ran into the driveway and jumped into the M Coupe.


I’ve been a pretty sane driver for decades, but if ever there was a time to burn rubber, this was it. I went around the left side of a guy at a red light, hung a right turn in front of him, ran the light, hit the entrance ramp to the Massachusetts Turnpike, and stood on it through three gears, plateauing just short of triple-digit speeds. I flew past everyone, even passing cars on the right when necessary, which I almost never do. I really try to make a point not to drive like an a$$hole in a BMW, but this time I was definitely that guy.


As the clock ticked past 7:25, I turned to Ethan and said, “I don’t think we’re going to make it.”


“I know, Dad,” he said dejectedly.


I don’t know if I was driving so fast that we experienced time dilation relative to the rest of the world, but when I got off at the exit in downtown Boston, the clock said 7:29. I made three right turns, then Ethan said, “That’s it! Stop the car! *STOP THE CAR!* ” He ran across the street and into the bar. I waited in the M Coupe.


I looked at my cell phone. It said 7:33. I was prepared to console a dejected child.


But a few minutes later, Ethan emerged with a Cheshire Cat grin on his face.


“You *made* it?”


“With 10 seconds to spare. I ran in, and there was huge applause as they were counting down the deadline. People hugged me and took my picture!”


We high-fived each other, then both just sat in the car and laughed our heads off. He called his crew and said that he’d made it. As we were driving back home (at far more sedate speeds), we deconstructed what we just did, and both marveled that *any* perturbation—a single red light—would’ve rocked things over the line to failure. Ethan said it was his favorite part of the film weekend.


When he got home, Ethan posted on Facebook (before he was too cool to have a Facebook account), “NOBODY drives like my dad.” I beamed with pride that I took my allocation of decades of insane driving I hadn’t done, let it out, and squeezed it into 12 minutes, and was able to do this for my kid.


The next day, Ethan told me that they were disqualified—the submitted film was unplayable because parts of it were still mistakenly linked to the source material on the hard drive instead of being embedded in the exported version. And since everything needed to be completed within 48 hours, “Oh, I’m sorry, I’ll drop off the right one,” wasn’t an option. Obviously, he was crushed, and his team was equally disappointed.


In the end, it wasn’t so bad. The film was still shown as part of the festival, although as a late submission it was ineligible for competition. And Ethan learned a valuable lesson about preparedness and time management.


But regarding me not having had a real “bonding experience” with the car, I was dead wrong. True, there was no long road trip. Not even a weekend getaway with my darling wife. But there was this. For 12 amazing minutes in the summer of 2010, in a silver M Coupe, father and son shared an adrenaline rush, slowed time, risked arrest, beat the odds and the clock, and nearly slipped the surly bonds of Earth. It was glorious, and neither of us will ever forget it.


Before Ethan moved out in 2012, I *did* let him drive the M Coupe once. He’s now 38, and has asked that, before the M Coupe departs the premises, he gets to drive it again. Maybe we’ll recreate our mad dash, this time at speeds that don’t bend space and slow time. Wouldn’t want to do anything, you know, foolish. I’ve used up that allocation.


Unless there’s another film on the line.


We’ll always have that time we were a$$holes in a BMW.


Rob Siegel


***
